summary: German has no single plural ending: there are five patterns, and the vowel often takes an umlaut (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü). -e: der Tisch – die Tische, der Stuhl – die Stühle. -er (with umlaut where possible): das Kind – die Kinder, das Buch – die Bücher. -(e)n: die Frau – die Frauen, die Lampe – die Lampen, die Lehrerin – die Lehrerinnen. -s (mostly loanwords and words ending in a vowel): das Handy – die Handys, das Baby – die Babys. No ending (often nouns in -er, -el, -chen): das Zimmer – die Zimmer, der Lehrer – die Lehrer, and with umlaut only: die Mutter – die Mütter, der Bruder – die Brüder. Learn every noun with its article and plural, as a dictionary gives it (der Stuhl, -e). The plural article is always die (dieser → diese, mein → meine), the indefinite article has no plural (ein Buch → Bücher), and in the dative plural the noun adds -n unless it already ends in -n or -s: den Kindern, but den Frauen, den Handys.

blocks.title: The dative plural adds -n
blocks.text: die Kinder → mit den Kindern, die Männer → den Männern, die Brüder → den Brüdern. No extra -n when the plural already ends in -n or -s: den Frauen, den Lampen, den Handys, den Omas.

blocks.title: Rules of thumb (not laws)
blocks.text: Feminine → usually -(e)n (and -in → -innen). Nouns in -chen, -lein, and masculine/neuter nouns in -er, -el, -en → no ending. Words from English or French, and nouns ending in a vowel other than -e → -s. One-syllable masculines → often -e, often with umlaut. One-syllable neuters → often -er with umlaut.

blocks.title: Plural only
blocks.text: die Leute (people), die Eltern (parents), die Großeltern (grandparents) have no singular: one person = eine Person, one parent = ein Elternteil.

askYourself: Which plural did I learn with this noun (der Stuhl, -e → die Stühle)?
Is it feminine? Then -(e)n is very likely; a female noun in -in takes -innen.
Does it end in -er, -el, -en or -chen (masculine or neuter)? Then no ending – maybe an umlaut (Mütter, Väter, Brüder).
Is it a loanword or does it end in a vowel (Handy, Baby, Opa)? Then often -s.
Is it a one-syllable neuter (Kind, Buch, Haus)? Then often -er with umlaut.
Is it dative plural? Add -n unless the plural already ends in -n or -s.
steps: Use die (nominative/accusative), den (dative) or der (genitive); no article for “some”.

traps: Umlaut only: die Mutter – die Mütter, der Vater – die Väter, der Bruder – die Brüder, die Tochter – die Töchter (die Muttern are nuts for bolts!).
Same form in the singular and plural: das Zimmer – die Zimmer, der Lehrer – die Lehrer, das Mädchen – die Mädchen, der Enkel – die Enkel.
Dative plural adds -n: den Kindern, den Männern – but not after -n or -s: den Frauen, den Handys.
Loanwords: das Baby – die Babys (not *Babies), der Cousin – die Cousins.
Weak masculines take -n everywhere: der Junge – die Jungen, der Neffe – die Neffen.
ein has no plural: ein Buch – Bücher (no article).
Leute, Eltern and Großeltern have no singular.

quiz.why: Masculine in -er: no ending (Lehrern is the dative plural).
Umlaut only; Muttern are nuts for bolts.

quiz.q: Which article goes with every plural noun?
quiz.why: die Stühle, die Lampen, die Bücher – one plural article for all three genders.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has a dual (two) and “broken” plurals made inside the word (kitāb → kutub) – a bigger version of German Buch → Bücher.
Hebrew plurals end mostly in -im (masculine) and -ot (feminine), with exceptions; the vowels inside the word often change too.
Chinese nouns do not change; numbers and measure words show the amount, 们 is added only for people.
After zwei and above the noun is plural: zwei Stühle, zehn Kinder.
